title: Does any fraction hit √2?
hook: With big enough numbers, surely some fraction hits √2 exactly?

knows: the diagonal of a 1-by-1 square is √2 (Pythagoras)
even and odd numbers; the idea of a proof by contradiction
doesNotKnow: why no fraction of whole numbers equals √2

misconception: With big enough whole numbers, some fraction will hit √2 exactly.
objective: The learner can explain that p/q = √2 would need p² = 2q², that 2q² keeps landing next to squares but never on one, and that the parity argument shows it never can.

claims.text: The diagonal of a 1-by-1 square is √2.
A fraction p/q equals √2 only if p² = 2 × q².
claims.source: Square both sides of p/q = √2 and multiply by q².

claims.text: For q from 1 to 70, 2 × q² is never a perfect square; the nearest square misses by exactly 1 at q = 1, 2, 5, 12, 29, 70 (for example 2 × 5² = 50 and 7² = 49). The reveal quotes the learner's own closest call (smallest miss, largest q among the q they tried).
claims.source: Recomputed with node for q = 1..70 (and no q up to 100000 gives a perfect square). The miss-by-1 values are the Pell numbers (solutions of p² - 2q² = ±1). The stage computes every value it shows from the same function. Illustration only: a table cannot prove it. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node with near(): q = 1..70 gives off 0 nowhere; off 1 exactly at 1, 2, 5, 12, 29, 70; 2 x 5^2 = 50, 7^2 = 49. BigInt check: no q up to 100,000 makes 2q^2 a perfect square. closest() sorts by off, then larger q, matching 'smallest miss, largest q'.

claims.text: A square p² has each factor 2 of p twice, so its count of 2s is even; 2 × q² has q's 2s twice plus one, so its count is odd. Even never equals odd, so no whole p and q give p² = 2 × q², and no fraction is √2.
claims.source: Classical parity proof, recorded in Aristotle, Prior Analytics I.23, and in later editions of Euclid's Elements (X, appendix); e.g. Hardy, A Mathematician's Apology, sec. 14. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own derivation: if p = 2^a m and q = 2^b n with m, n odd, p^2 has 2a factors 2 and 2q^2 has 2b+1 (2 is prime, so counts add under multiplication); even never equals odd, so p^2 = 2q^2 has no whole solution. Cited Aristotle/Euclid/Hardy not opened; note they give the lowest-terms form of the proof, not this count-of-2s form. The sentence rests on the derivation.

claims.text: If p/q = sqrt(2), squaring both sides gives p^2 = 2 x q^2.
claims.source: (p/q)^2 = 2 multiplied by q^2; same fact as c2, now with the squaring step stated on the stage. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 11): (p/q)^2 = 2, times q^2: p^2 = 2q^2. The multiply step is implicit in "gives"; acceptable.

claims.text: The stage labels each square with its count of factor 2s, always even (e.g. 16² = 256 has 8, 7² = 49 has 0), and labels 2 × q² with its count, always odd (e.g. 2 × 5² = 50 has 1, 2 × 12² = 288 has 5).
claims.source: twos() in Demo.tsx counts factors of 2. If q = 2^a × m with m odd, q² = 2^(2a) × m², so 2q² = 2^(2a+1) × m²: odd count. Any p² = 2^(2b) × (odd)²: even count. 256 = 2^8, 49 odd, 50 = 2 × 25, 288 = 2^5 × 9. By unique factorisation p² = 2q² is impossible (the same fact as the lowest-terms parity proof). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node with twos(): 256 has 8, 49 has 0, 50 has 1, 288 has 5; for every q in 1..70 both bracketing squares have even counts and 2q^2 odd. 16^2 is shown at q = 12 (288 between 256 and 289), 7^2 at q = 5. Stage labels '2s: n (even)' and '2s: n (odd)'.

recall.question: A friend says: 'My computer found p and q, each with a million digits, so that p/q is exactly √2.' What do you say?
options: Impossible: p² = 2q² would force p and q both even, forever
Possible, if the numbers are big enough
Possible, but only with a computer
recall.why: Exact equality needs p² = 2q². That makes p even, then q even, so the fraction can always be reduced: no lowest-terms fraction works, at any size.
